title: How AI helped me untangle an NES game from its hardware
partialText:
From 6502 assembly to maintainable JavaScript, and what a second AI assistant revealed about the behavior we had left behind.

Disclosure: AI assistants contributed to the analysis of the original code, implementation and testing of the JavaScript port, and the drafting and editing of this article. I directed the investigation, reviewed the evidence and take responsibility for the findings and conclusions.

Could I turn a Nintendo Entertainment System game into a maintainable browser application without embedding an emulator? I wanted ordinary JavaScript that I could read and change, while keeping the game faithful not only in appearance but in behavior.

The game was Lawn Mower, a 2011 homebrew by Shiru. You steer a mower that never stops, cut every patch of grass and collect fuel cans before the tank runs dry. Stones and flowers make that harder. I chose it for Libre Arcade, my software preservation project for older open games. The aim is to document the original sources and provenance, then give these games a future as browser applications rather than depend on their original hardware.

Shiru had released the game and its source code into the public domain, allowing the original work to be preserved and ported without negotiating a separate license.

ChatGPT helped me investigate the source and build the first JavaScript port. I then passed the ROM, code and test package to Claude Code with a different task: measure where our port disagreed with the original. That second pass rewrote substantial parts of the application. The story became as much about how we established correctness as about how we made the game run.

A tiny ROM carried more than code and graphics

We recovered Shiru’s competition ROM, labelled Lawn Mower v1.1 30.05.11, and a later source archive, version 1.12, written in 6502 assembly for NESASM. The archive included graphics, music data, levels and development material.

The original ROM occupies just 24,592 bytes: a 16-byte iNES header, 16 KiB of PRG-ROM and 8 KiB of CHR-ROM. PRG contains 6502 instructions and data; CHR is usually associated with the 8 × 8 pixel patterns drawn by the NES. Lawn Mower uses mapper 0, so the cartridge needs no bank-switching logic.

The surprising part was inside CHR. Alongside the tiles sit ten level records, 95 bytes each, beginning at CHR offset $1000. A graphics-only extraction would have missed the level maps. Even in a simple mapper 0 cartridge, finding the game means identifying what the bytes mean, not just which chip holds them.

An assembly listing supplies operations, not explanations. A memory address might hold the fuel counter, a temporary arithmetic value or the controller state. A branch might enforce a rule or depend on a flag left by another routine. The source tells you what the CPU executes, not what the game is supposed to do.

There was also no single unquestionable “original”. The competition ROM and the later 1.12 build have identical CHR data, but their program sections differ in thousands of bytes, partly because the code moved. Rebuilding the later ROM turned into a separate exercise in tool archaeology. The assembler first used in the Lawn Mower investigation produced a different binary. A NESASM-compatible assembler developed during the restoration of another game, Lan Master, was then corrected to handle a subtle addressing rule. With that assembler, the source produced a 24,592-byte ROM identical to the archived author build, with zero different bytes. This establishes the provenance of the source more firmly, but does not resolve every timing comparison made earlier with a different assembler. A reproducible build and a matching execution trace are separate results.

AI made the first reconstruction practical

The first task was semantic porting. Rather than translate the PRG into JavaScript instruction by instruction, I used ChatGPT to help work through the assembly routines and turn them into an explicit model of the game. We reconstructed the rules for steering, movement, collisions, cutting grass, consuming fuel, collecting cans and advancing through ten lawns. We kept the original data and numeric conventions where they mattered, but gave the application a structure built for the browser.

The new program separated the game kernel from the presentation layer. Canvas replaced the NES graphics pipeline. Web Audio reproduced the game’s music and effects. Keyboard and touch controls took the place of the controller. The resulting code was not a wrapper around a ROM. It was an application that could run without a virtual NES.

In the original, a stone’s fuel penalty is arithmetic over 8-bit state. In JavaScript it can become a named, testable rule. That is a practical gain in maintainability.

This work would have been possible without AI. I did not run a controlled comparison, so I cannot attach a percentage to the time saved. But the assistants made it practical for me to move repeatedly between a large assembly listing, binary assets, JavaScript modules and tests, and to keep refining the result across milestones. AI helped with interpretation and implementation. It did not automatically extract a perfect specification from the code.

Recovering the game’s rules was only part of the challenge. For example, hitting a stone removes 77 units of fuel from a maximum of 232. Expressing that rule in JavaScript is straightforward. But reproducing the original behavior also means knowing when the collision is processed, which frames actually advance the game, and how seemingly unrelated operations affect what happens next. Even visual effects consume values from the same random number generator used to place fuel cans. Two implementations can follow the same rules and still produce different games if they execute those rules in a different order.

You can remove the console without removing its effects

A semantic port does not need to keep a PPU or an APU running inside the application. But the NES’s hardware behavior can still be part of the game’s behavior, and removing the hardware does not make those dependencies disappear.

We learned this gradually. Earlier release candidates showed black bands, title lettering broken across horizontal lines and messages drawn with the wrong graphics bank. Some fixes required understanding exactly where the original changed its scroll or pattern settings during a frame. Drawing the same tiles in Canvas was not enough; the transitions and ordering mattered too.

Other effects are harder to spot. NES sprites have priorities, with no more than eight rendered per scanline. The original fades through palette changes, not a black overlay. Its frame counter can advance while the display is off, and later movement or fuel consumption may depend on that count. A visual transition can change gameplay state.

A playable port was not proof of fidelity

By RC6, the port was playable and 87 tests passed. The suite caught regressions in reconstructed rules and previously fixed defects.

It did not mean we had proved equivalence with the ROM. Many of the tests checked JavaScript expectations against JavaScript results. Visual checks could compare the page with reference images generated by our own code. Such tests detect regressions in the implementation, but they can preserve a mistaken interpretation just as effectively as a correct one.

So I handed Claude Code the ROM, source, application and reports, asking whether the original made the same decisions under the same inputs. The port was now a hypothesis to challenge. The work that followed changed the code as well as the evidence.

I could have continued with ChatGPT for this second phase. Switching to Claude Code was not a controlled comparison between AI models. The important change was the assignment: instead of improving a playable port, I wanted to test its assumptions against the original executable.

Claude Code’s reported solution was to build a small NES execution environment specifically for the investigation. It included a 6502 core with cycle accounting, relevant memory mapping, controller reads, interrupts, PPU state and a log of writes to graphics registers. The harness could run the original ROM while the JavaScript port received an equivalent controller sequence.

At every NMI, the two executions were compared on game variables, video memory, palette and sprite state, and bytes delivered to the audio hardware. Claude Code also built a frame compositor that reconstructed the original game’s visuals from the NES graphics memory and a log of PPU register writes. The reconstructed frames were then compared pixel by pixel with the JavaScript renderer, excluding the few scanlines where the original changed graphics registers mid-line. This made the original executable an oracle: not an idealized description of what the game ought to do, but a concrete reference for what its code actually did under the tested conditions.

The test records describe roughly 455,000 frames checked against each of three programs: the competition ROM, the author’s v1.12 ROM, and the program assembled from the source, covering random inputs, fuel exhaustion and level progression. They also describe thirteen faults deliberately introduced into the JavaScript port, each detected by the oracle. These are results of the later Lawn Mower audit, not of the earlier 87-test JavaScript suite. I have not rerun that full oracle suite for this article. The NES runner was built for the investigation, so spot checks against an established emulator would provide a further independent reference.

Claude Code did more than add tests. It kept much of the recovered game data and gameplay logic, but substantially rewrote the rendering system and parts of the application. The second pass built on the first implementation without treating it as an authoritative specification.

The bugs that mattered most were not obvious bugs

One reported discovery involved the rate at which Lawn Mower updates its game logic. On NTSC hardware it generally skips a logic update every fifth interrupt. The first port implemented the apparent rule directly. In the assembly, however, the decision depends on the X register at the end of the loop. A routine searching for a position for the next fuel can does not restore X, so after that search an update that might otherwise be skipped can run. The program’s behavior depends on an incidental register value, not just on the tidy rule we inferred.

Input handling exposed a similar problem. A browser delivers keyboard events when keys are pressed or released. The NES program samples its controller in particular loops and detects a fresh button press relative to its previous read. That distinction affects pausing, continuing and acknowledging the ending. The original also has a title-screen level skip sequence that the initial port omitted. A correct button mapping did not, by itself, reproduce the original’s input semantics.

The random generator was simpler as code and more difficult as behavior. Its core is only a few operations:

const carry = (seed >>> 7) & 1;
seed = (seed << 1) & 0xff;
if (carry) seed ^= 0xcf;

But the seed is initialized on a cold reset, and the original consumes the sequence during the title screen as well as during play. Fuel cans, grass variations and effects such as mower debris share the generator. Drawing one decorative effect at a different moment can change which value is used for the next fuel can. Separating visual randomness from gameplay randomness would be sensible in a new game, but it would not reproduce this one.

The ROM-based comparison also exposed errors in sprite ordering, palette fades and transition controls. One timing difference remains unresolved. When entering the fifth lawn, Shiru’s v1.12 ROM sometimes keeps the display disabled for ten NMIs rather than nine, while the browser port always uses nine. A difference in instruction layout may explain the extra frame, but this has not yet been confirmed by a cycle-level trace using the byte-identical build.

The apparent meaning of a routine was not its complete meaning. Register contents, controller timing and the order in which visual effects consumed random numbers could change the outcome. Recovering intent was only half the job; we also needed to preserve the consequences of execution.

An oracle can reveal mistakes without proving everything

Running the ROM alongside the port gives better evidence than testing the port alone, but it cannot prove universal equivalence. A custom emulator may have mistakes, and an untested input can still expose a divergence. The reported visual tests do not capture every within-scanline change. Audio is compared at the level of chip inputs, not measured browser waveforms; palette and NTSC timing choices impose other limits.

There is a more basic question, too: which original do we mean? The competition version 1.1 and the later 1.12 build do not agree on every tiny transitional behavior. The integration followed v1.12 by default and retained a switch, checkPadClearsDirection, for the v1.1 behavior. I did not explicitly choose that default at the time. An oracle can reveal the differences, but it cannot make the historical choice on our behalf. If a default is going to stand as an editorial decision, it needs to be made and recorded as one.

An oracle makes uncertainty visible and turns disagreements into reproducible tests. That is more useful than declaring the work finished.

Compiling the instructions did not recover the rule

Before deciding whether to attempt a whole-game recompilation, I wanted a direct comparison with the semantic port. A static recompiler turns identified machine instructions into host code, usually with an additional runtime to model the console. Emulation instead runs the original ROM on a model of the machine. Semantic porting writes a new implementation of the recovered behavior. They answer related but different questions.

I read the documentation for NESRecomp and NES Recompiled, but did not run either tool on Lawn Mower. NESRecomp’s PolyForm Noncommercial license is a further obstacle to including its runtime in the freely redistributable Libre Arcade collection. The smaller C experiment below used our own explicitly limited opcode translator, not either project.

To understand the difference, I returned to a very ordinary event in Lawn Mower: hitting a stone. In the original assembly, cutStone sets a camera-shake flag, loads the fuel penalty and calls fuelSubtract. That second routine uses the 6502 carry flag to subtract without going below zero. It also checks whether the fuel counter has just crossed the low-fuel threshold, in which case it requests a warning sound. The collision then requests the stone effect. The penalty is 77, but the full behavior is more than a subtraction.

cutStone
    lda #1
    sta <GAME_CAM_SHAKE
    lda #GAME_FUEL_MAX/3
    jsr fuelSubtract
    lda #SFX_STONE
    jmp sfxPlay

I tried a deliberately small static translation experiment using the ROM bytes rather than treating the assembly as executable evidence. A Python script found the actual opcode sequences for cutStone and fuelSubtract in both the competition ROM (v1.1) and Shiru's later v1.12 release. It decoded those instructions into C branches and state updates, compiled the result with GCC and ran it against the final JavaScript kernel that came out of the Claude Code pass. The two calls to the original sound routines were treated as observable event boundaries; I did not recompile those sound routines or the NES hardware.

For each ROM, I checked every fuel value from 0 to 232. I compared the fuel remaining, camera shake, the low-fuel warning and the stone event. All 233 cases agreed. I then changed the penalty from 77 to 60 in a temporary copy of each instruction stream, made the matching one-line change to a temporary copy of the JavaScript constant, and repeated the sweep. Across the two ROM versions and both penalties, 932 of 932 state-and-event comparisons agreed. This verifies the bounded collision routine under those inputs, not a recompiled playable NES game. The script, the generated C and the traces are published here.

The contrast is visible in the resulting code. The generated C still operates on a byte of memory at $CB, a carry flag and branches to instruction addresses. It reproduces the operations, but it does not know that $CB is the fuel counter. In JavaScript, the same behavior sits behind STONE_PENALTY, subtractFuel() and a stone-hit event. A developer can recognize the rule immediately. Yet that clarity is not automatic proof of fidelity: the first JavaScript port was readable too, and it had missed other side effects of the original machine.

This is where recompilation and semantic porting meet rather than compete. Static translation can retain execution details that are easy to overlook while rewriting; semantic porting can give those details names and separable responsibilities. Neither one settles correctness alone. For that, I still need the original ROM and a test that can disagree with my reconstruction.

A second game suggested the method could travel

A separate restoration of Concentration Room, a 2010 NES memory game by Damian Yerrick, followed a similar approach. The first JavaScript port came with passing tests, but those tests relied largely on assumptions drawn from the source code rather than comparisons with the running game. Claude Code then used the original croom.nes as a reference, comparing game state and reconstructed images during scripted play.

For Concentration Room, the comparison covered 174 game-state fields at each iteration of the original game loop. Across 64 scenarios and 128 games, the oracle checked 310,756 iterations, while visual comparisons covered 119,426 frames.

We also deliberately introduced 30 faults into the JavaScript port to test whether the oracle could detect them. It caught 28, revealing two gaps in our test coverage. Unlike the Lawn Mower audit, the Concentration Room oracle did not compare the values sent to the NES sound registers. The original music and sound data were verified against the ROM, but the browser’s synthesized audio was not compared with the console’s output.

The complete source code, test tools and archaeological documentation are preserved in Libre Arcade.

This time the defects involved direction handlers reordered by shuffle.py -r, input during CPU turns, lingering state after a game and two incorrectly transcribed music notes. The same method exposed different misunderstandings.

Each pass changed what I could verify

What began as a readable reconstruction became a testable claim about the original program. I no longer had to rely on whether the port looked right or behaved as I expected. I could ask where it differed from the original, frame by frame, and use those differences to improve the implementation.

There was a human role throughout. I chose the restoration target, required a final application without an embedded NES emulator, supplied historical artifacts and reviewed the evidence. I also learned that one choice had escaped explicit review: the integration adopted v1.12 behavior by default, with a switch for the competition version. That is precisely the kind of decision a restoration should record rather than attribute to its author after the fact. The tools can recover code and produce tests; they do not settle what counts as the canonical game.

The same problem appears in old parsers, batch programs and simulations. AI can help recover a model and move it to a new platform. Establishing which old details are part of the system’s actual contract still requires a reference executable, careful comparison and a willingness to revise the rewrite.

The provenance notes, oracle harness, ROM comparison tests and sensitivity tests show how the original executable was used to check the browser port.

Can AI help recover the logic of an old game and give it a life beyond its original hardware?

In Lawn Mower, it helped. We got closer to the original only when we started checking the new code against what the old ROM actually did.

title: Let’s Build Our Own Mutex in Rust
partialText:
Parallelization is an easy way to make a program faster, at the cost of increased complexity.

In Rust, the easiest way to deal with said complexity is with a Mutex.

You just wrap your data in a Mutex, and call .lock() to get a reference… It’s like magic!

But it’s not magic. In fact, you can make your own in just 122 lines of Rust; treating Mutexes like magic means you might be missing out on major performance boosts.

So… how do Mutexes work in the first place?
How do we make one?
And how can understanding their internals help us write more efficient concurrent Rust?

Why do we need a Mutex?

Data races occur when two or more threads access the same variable, at least one is attempting to write, and there is no synchronization employed.

Most operations on a given variable have three steps:

  1. Load the data from memory into a register
  2. Do some work on the register
  3. Store the register back into memory

If two threads execute these steps concurrently, both might read the same old value before either writes its update. This can cause one update to be lost, producing an incorrect result.

Atomics

Atomic operations avoid data races by providing two guarantees:

  1. They are Indivisible (either not started or complete; never in-process)
  2. They are Ordered (certain operations can be guaranteed to precede others)

Collectively, these prevent threads from working with an incorrect or invalid version of the variable. In Rust, we can use atomic operations via std::sync::atomic.

Here’s what using one looks like in code:

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU16, Ordering};
fn main() {
  let counter = AtomicU16::new(0);
  counter.fetch_add(10, Ordering::Relaxed); //atomically adds 10 to counter
  println!("{:?}", counter); //counter = counter + 10;
}
What is Ordering?
The compiler (during compilation) and the CPU (during execution) take lots of liberty in what happens when. We’ll revisit Ordering a little later in depth. For now, just know that Ordering::Relaxed provides no synchronization — the compiler and CPU may move operations before and after Relaxed atomic operations at will in the current thread. It’s used when we’re using atomic values simply to store data (such as incrementing a counter) and not as a flag to access other data (as we will do later).

Atomics are implemented on the CPU level which means they are quick and lightweight (no additional memory required).

The downside with Atomics, though, is that they are extremely limited: since atomic operations are dependent on the CPU, only a handful of types are supported (primarily AtomicBool, AtomicPtr, AtomicUsize, and a handful of AtomicInt variants).

More specifically: atomic operations must be on specific, known, and fixed memory lengths. The allowed lengths are dependent on the CPU.

So, when we can use Atomics, we almost always should… but when we can’t (for example, with an unsupported type like a Vec), how would we share data between threads?

Locks

Remember, data races can only happen when there are more than one thread accessing the same memory at the same instant, so we can prevent them by only allowing one thread access at a time and making any other threads that want access wait.

The most obvious idea is to make a struct storing a boolean flag is_locked alongside the data itself:

  1. Whenever a thread wants to read or write, we check is_locked
  2. If is_lockedis false, no threads are currently accessing the data inside. The struct gives the thread a pointer to the data inside. This is called locking the variable.
  3. Whenever a thread is done with writing/reading, we set is_lockedto false, allowing other threads to work with the data. This is called unlocking.
  4. If is_lockedis true, this means there is another thread accessing the data. We keep on checking is_lockeduntil it becomes false, at which point we can safely provide a pointer to our data.

The actual implementation is a little more complicated, though:

  1. We need to use an AtomicBool to avoid a data race on the value of the bool itself.
  2. If we want to share our Lock class between threads, it must be an immutable reference. While we can get an immutable reference (&T) to a mutable pointer (*mut T) via a type cast, it can lead to undefined behaviour in Rust; Rust typically assumes that data reachable through a shared reference (&T) is not mutated, unless that mutation happens through an approved interior-mutability mechanism. Therefore, the simplest way is wrapping T in UnsafeCell and using UnsafeCell.get() to safely convert &T to *mut T.

Here’s the general outline of our Lock struct:

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};
use std::cell::UnsafeCell;

struct Lock<T> {
  is_locked: AtomicBool,
  data: UnsafeCell<T>
}
 
impl<T> Lock<T> {
  fn new(data: T) -> Self {
    Self {
      data: UnsafeCell::new(data),
      is_locked: AtomicBool::new(false) //starts unlocked
    }
  }

  fn lock(&self) -> *mut T {
    todo!();
  }

  fn unlock(&self) {
    todo!();
  }
}

.lock needs to check if is_locked is false, and if so set it to true.
Usually we’d do something along the lines of:

if !is_locked {
  is_locked = true;
} else {
  //further code
}

but we can’t, because that operation is not atomic; just because something is wrapped in an Atomic doesn’t mean working with it is always threadsafe.

We still need to make sure our operations are indivisible; the above snippet is not. Before one thread has written is_locked to true, a second thread may read is_locked as false.

Rather than using a typical if-statement we must use compare_exchange, which does three things:

  1. compares is_locked’s value with a desired value
  2. if they are equal, it exchanges is_locked with a provided value
  3. returns the new value of is_locked wrapped in a Result(Okif the compare passed, otherwise Err).

compare_exchange also takes an Ordering. Our lock provides thread safety by providing only one thread a pointer to the data at the time; however, the compiler and CPU like to shift around operations for efficiency, leading to a scenario where simultaneous writes happen.

Therefore, we must ensure the correct access ordering by providing the correct Ordering:

  • Ordering::Relaxed: no synchronization or access ordering
  • Ordering::Release: code before the atomic operation cannot slide past the atomic operation; everything must be wrapped up first.
  • Ordering::Acquire: code after the atomic operation cannot slide before the atomic operation; everything must wait for the atomic operation
  • Ordering::AcqRel: a combination of the previous two.
  • Ordering::SeqCst (Sequentially consistent): synchronizes operations between threads so that there is one sequentially consistent ordering of events

For locking, what Ordering would we use?

It’s helpful to think of what shared data the thread can access before and after the compare_exchange. There isn’t anything relevant before, but after the lock operation a thread gains access to Lock.data, which is being shared across multiple threads. We never want to access Lock.data before lock occurs, so we must use Ordering::Acquire.

compare_exchange also asks for a failure Ordering; it allows us to have good performance when the compare check fails. Again, what shared data can the thread access before/after a failed compare_exchange in our case? None; the compare must pass to lock, so we can use the least restrictive (and most performant) Ordering::Relaxed.

Now we’re can write the lock operation:

use std::sync::atomic::Ordering;

fn lock(&self) -> *mut T {
  while self.is_locked.compare_exchange(
    false, //expected
    true, //new value
    Ordering::Acquire, //success ordering
    Ordering::Relaxed, //failure ordering
  ).is_err() { } //compare_exchange returns Err(previous value) if the compare fails.
   
  self.data.get()
}

Our unlock operation only requires an atomic store operation. As it’s being used to demarcate the end of access to the inner data, we use Ordering::Release:

fn unlock(&self) {
  self.is_locked.store(false, Ordering::Release);
}

Finally, we need to implement the Send and Sync traits.

| Send and Sync are invariants: we are assuring the compiler that Lock’s strategy for accessing data is fully thread safe. There is no code involved, but because the compiler cannot check our work easily, these traits are unsafe.

unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for Lock<T> {}
unsafe impl<T: Send> Send for Lock<T> {}
This version of the lock can be found in src/lock.rs

We Now Have a Working Lock!

It’s a little unsafe though.

Most literally, every single time we want to use our pointer, we need an unsafe block. But also: what if someone just… forgets to call unlock? Any threads trying to access the data would just spin forever!

We can use the idea of Guards to resolve both of these issues. Essentially, rather than returning a raw pointer, we’ll return a smart pointer that automatically calls unlock before going out of scope.

Our Guard will simply contain a reference to the lock.

struct LockGuard<'a, T> {
  lock: &'a Lock<T>,
}

We add two methods to LockGuard; new, and unlock:

impl<'a, T> LockGuard<'a, T> {
  fn new(lock: &'a Lock<T>) -> Self {
    LockGuard {
      lock
    }
  }
  
  fn unlock(self) {}
}

It’s important that we remove Lock.unlock; it can be called multiple times per Lock.lock(potentially leading to bugs) while LockGuard.unlock consumes LockGuard and therefore can only be called once per guard.

unlock is intentionally a no-op, though… why?

We’re implement Drop to unlock the mutex when the guard goes out of scope:

use std::ops::Drop;
 
impl<'a, T> Drop for LockGuard<'a, T>{
  fn drop(&mut self) {
    self.lock.unlock();
  }
}

Drop is always called when a struct goes out of scope. This happens automatically in our unlock function, as self is moved into the function and goes out of scope when the function is done… so our unlock function doesn’t need a single line of code!

And finally, we implement Deref and DerefMut so that we can cleanly obtain both immutable and mutable references:

use std::ops::{Deref, DerefMut};

impl<'a, T> Deref for LockGuard<'a, T> {
  type Target = T;
  fn deref(&self) -> &Self::Target {
    unsafe { &*self.lock.data.get() }
  }
}

impl<'a, T> DerefMut for LockGuard<'a, T> {
  fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Self::Target {
    unsafe { &mut *self.lock.data.get() }
  }
}
Now, we simply modify Lock.unlock to return a LockGuard. This is omitted for brevity but can be found in src/guarded_lock.rs.

This Lock is Not a Mutex

We haven’t actually implemented a Mutex; we’ve implemented a Spin Lock.

What is the difference between them anyway?

They are both locks that synchronize access to data (making it thread safe), and they both use an atomic flag internally, however the strategies they use are slightly different:

  • When the compare exchange in our Spin Lock fails, we simply loop again — this is called spinning.
  • When the compare exchange in a Mutex fails, the thread is added to a queue of threads who wish to access the data. It sleeps and is woken by the Mutex when the current writer relinquishes their reference through unlock.

It’s a minor difference, but it makes a notable impact. To understand this, we need to understand the difference between threads and cores. Cores are physical hardware units, while threads are streams of tasks that a core needs to do.

We can have more threads than cores; that just means cores need to rapidly switch between two threads. By having a core sleep (rather than spin), more time (per cycle) can be used on threads which are actually doing computation, allowing our program to finish quicker.

From now on, for clarity and accuracy, we’ll call our Lock and LockGuard structs SpinLock and SpinLockGuard, respectively. I’ll refer to them by their updated names going forward.

The Recipe for a DIY Mutex

Remember: unlike a Spin Lock, a Mutex manages the line of threads that want access to the lock. Specifically, threads that are waiting for access to some data are put to sleep, and unlocking wakes a thread- we’ll need a list to store each sleeping thread. The important thing, though, is that we cannot use a regular list.

Because the list of queues will be shared across threads, it can be subject to data races as well (for example, if two threads try to call .append at the same time). Lists cannot be made atomic, so we can simply use our previously made SpinLock to access the list across threads.

Because of spurious wake ups (the thread may wake up before we call .unpark), we’ll still need to control access to our internal data with an atomic to ensure only one thread tries to access it at a time.

This is the layout of our mutex.

use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicBool, Ordering};
use std::cell::UnsafeCell;
use std::thread;
use std::ops::{Drop, Deref, DerefMut};
use std::collections::VecDeque;

struct MyMutex<T> {
  data: UnsafeCell<T>,
  is_locked: AtomicBool,
  queue: SpinLock<VecDeque<thread::Thread>> //thread::Thread is a handle to a thread so it can be unparked
}

impl<T> MyMutex<T> {
  fn new(inner_data: T) -> Self {
    MyMutex {
      data: UnsafeCell::new(inner_data),
      is_locked: AtomicBool::new(false),
      queue: SpinLock::new(VecDeque::new())
    }
  }

  fn lock<'a>(&'a self) -> MyMutexGuard<'a, T> {
    todo!();
  }
}

struct MyMutexGuard<'a, T> {
  mutex: &'a MyMutex<T>,
}

impl<'a, T> Drop for MyMutexGuard<'a, T>{
  fn drop(&mut self) {
    todo!();
  }
}
//other MyMutexGuard impls (MyMutexGuard::new, .unlock, Deref, DerefMut) omitted for brevity
//also, .unlock is still a no-op here
Most of the implementation of MyMutexGuard is the exact same as SpinLockGuard… we omit it here but you can find it in src/mymutex.rs

For lock:

  1. We first try a compare_exchange. If it succeeds we obtain a reference to the protected data in the form of a MyMutexGuard.
  2. Otherwise, we add the thread’s handle to the queue
  3. We can park the thread once we’ve ensured is_locked hasn’t changed since our previous check
  4. When the thread wakes, or if is_locked has changed, we go back to step 1
fn lock<'a>(&'a self) -> MyMutexGuard<'a, T> {
  let current = thread::current();

  loop {
    if self.is_locked.compare_exchange(
      false, //expected
      true, //new value
      Ordering::Acquire, //success ordering
      Ordering::Relaxed, //failure ordering
    ).is_ok() {
      //we have access
      return MyMutexGuard::new(self);
    }

    let mut ptr = self.queue.lock();
    ptr.push_back(current.clone());
    ptr.unlock();
    
    if self.is_locked.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
      //check whether is_locked changed between the last check & joining the queue
      //SeqCst used to sync wakeups from other threads with the load operation
      thread::park();
      //we only pass this line after the thread wakes
    } else {
      let mut ptr = self.queue.lock();
      ptr.retain(|x| x .id() != current.id()); //remove us from queue & repeat
    }
}
Here, compare_exchange has the exact same memory ordering as SpinLock

MyMutexGuard.Drop is the same as SpinLockGuard.Drop with the addition of logic to wake threads in the queue:

impl<'a, T> Drop for MyMutexGuard<'a, T> {
  fn drop(&mut self) {
    self.mutex.is_locked.store(false, Ordering::Release);
    let ptr = self.mutex.queue.lock();
    if ptr.len() > 0 {
      ptr.pop_front().unwrap().unpark();
    }
    //remember, we don't even have to unlock… our SpinLockGuard does it for us
  }
}

And finally we implement Send & Sync :

unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for MyMutex<T> {}
unsafe impl<T: Send> Send for MyMutex<T> {}

But all this is extremely similar to our Spin Lock. Will there even be a significant difference in performance?

Let’s See

We’ll benchmark a task that lets us vary contention (the number of threads calling lock at a time) and critical section length (how long the lock is locked for).

We have 10 separately locked lists, each of length L, and T threads. Each thread reverses one list that is deterministically assigned to it. If T > 64, multiple threads will try to reverse the same list. Contention should be proportional to T/10 and critical section length proportional to N.

The code was optimized before benchmarking; only a handful of changes were made. The source code contains all the modifications.

It’s not that cut and dry after all; when only one or two threads are accessing the data, SpinLock is much faster. On the other hand, MyMutex is faster when contention is higher.

This is because the overhead of putting a thread to sleep can only be justified when lots of threads would otherwise be spinning. So, next time you write some multi-threaded code, don’t just drop in a Mutex. Perhaps an Atomic, or a Spin Lock from an external crate, or one of Rust’s many other synchronization primitives (SeqLock, RwLock,…) would do better?

Let’s also benchmark our MyMutex against the Mutex from Rust’s standard library for the same task to make sure it isn’t extremely unoptimized.

Yes, it’s quite neck-and-neck, but of course there are a few regions in which our MyMutex does worse. And this is to be expected; we’ve hardly done any optimizations. A production-level mutex might use a Futex, for example, which delegates management of the queue of sleeping threads to the OS.

And we’ve done all this in just 222 lines of Rust (excluding empty lines), 122 if we’re counting only the mutex implementation — so mutexes aren’t magic, after all.

Do note: what we’ve implemented is not a production-ready mutex. Production-level mutexes require proofs of correctness and tests under various loads and settings.

Again, all code can be found here

Thanks for reading! I hope you’ve learnt a lot about synchronization, locking, and Rust; leave a clap if this helped!

Till next time,

Ein Monarch

title: From Pixels to Vectors: Image Embeddings in Practice
partialText:
How to optimize storage with embeddings and learn the technique through a practical project

In the previous article, we learned a little more about embeddings, how context became encoded in these representations following advances brought by Transformers, and how to measure distances between words.

How to Measure Similarity Between SQL Queries Using Embeddings

In this article, we will take things one step further by applying the same principle to images.

But what about images?

I have always enjoyed learning through practical examples. So, we will work on something we can implement and use in our daily lives.

Unlike the days when an analog film gave us only 36 shots, the number of pictures we can take with our phones today is virtually unlimited. It is not unusual to find a folder containing hundreds or thousands of files — or someone whose phone storage is full because of an overcrowded photo gallery. In these situations, we often have consecutive pictures of the same scene, the same image in different resolutions, or files that look very similar.

With only a few images, we can open them one by one and decide which ones to keep. However, as the collection grows, manual analysis becomes tedious and difficult to scale. This is where image embeddings can help us.

Isn’t an image just a matrix of pixels?

To a computer, an image is already a set of numbers: a matrix formed by its pixel values. However, comparing these values directly is not very robust, because compression, resizing, or a small crop can change many pixels without changing what we actually see.

Therefore, the right comparison depends on the question we want to answer:

- Are the files the same?
- Do the images appear to be the same photograph?
- Do the images represent similar concepts?

A cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 helps answer the first question. A perceptual hash such as pHash is useful for the second. Embeddings are especially interesting for the third.

What is an image embedding?

As explained in the first article, an embedding transforms information into a vector representation that preserves important characteristics of its meaning. In that case, we worked with text and queries; now, we will do the same with images.

After passing through an encoder, each photograph is represented by a vector. When we place these vectors in the same space, we can calculate how close they are to one another: beach images tend to be close to other beach images, while car photographs may occupy a different region. The same photograph at different resolutions tends to be even closer, although the result depends on the encoder being used.

To create these representations, we need to choose a model capable of understanding visual features. This is where CLIP comes in.

CLIP: bringing images and text closer together

In this experiment, we will use the clip-ViT-B-32 model, available through the sentence-transformers library.

CLIP is particularly interesting because it was trained to bring matching images and text descriptions closer together in a shared space. This creates possibilities that go beyond comparing two photographs. In a more complete application, we could search for images using a sentence such as “a dog playing in the park,” even if that text had never been stored in the file’s metadata.

In our case, we will focus on comparing images. We will use CLIP’s encoder to generate the embeddings and place them in a vector space, where we can calculate the similarity between the images.

Let’s get to the project

Now that we have defined the problem and understand how embeddings can help, we will use Python 3.10 or later to build our solution. We will also need a few libraries for image processing, mathematical operations, and working with Transformers.

Although I will explain the main steps below, the complete project is available on GitHub:

GitHub - Lucs1590/image-embedding-lab

We begin by locating the images that will be processed. The code scans the selected folder and its subdirectories, considering formats such as JPG, PNG, WEBP, BMP, and TIFF.

SUPPORTED_EXTENSIONS = {
    ".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".webp",
    ".bmp", ".tif", ".tiff"
}

def list_images(input_dir: Path) -> list[Path]:
    paths = sorted(
        path
        for path in input_dir.rglob("*")
        if path.is_file()
        and path.suffix.lower() in SUPPORTED_EXTENSIONS
    )
    if len(paths) < 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Esperava ao menos 2 imagens em {input_dir}, "
            f"encontrei {len(paths)}."
        )
    return paths

Loading the images correctly

Before passing an image to the model, we perform two important operations. The first is to respect its EXIF orientation, preventing photographs taken with a phone from being processed with the wrong rotation. The second is to convert it to RGB, ensuring a consistent input format.

def load_rgb(path: Path) -> Image.Image:
    with Image.open(path) as image:
        return ImageOps.exif_transpose(image).convert("RGB")

This function may look simple, but it prevents several unexpected behaviors. In a more robust application, we would also need to handle corrupted files, unexpected formats, and excessively large images during decoding.

Generating the embeddings

With the images prepared, we load `clip-ViT-B-32` and call its `encode` method. If a CUDA-compatible GPU is available, it will be used. Otherwise, the processing will run on the CPU, although this computationally intensive step may take considerably longer.

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
model = SentenceTransformer("clip-ViT-B-32", device=device)

batch_embeddings = model.encode(
    images,
    batch_size=batch_size,
    normalize_embeddings=True,
    show_progress_bar=False,
)

The normalize_embeddings=True parameter makes each vector have a norm of 1. This simplifies the calculation performed later, because the dot product of two normalized vectors is equivalent to their cosine similarity.

In simple terms, each image is no longer just a grid of pixels: it becomes a point in a high-dimensional space.

Necessary optimizations

An initial version of the project could load every image into memory, generate all the embeddings, and then compare every vector. This works for a small example. However, as the volume grows, three problems quickly appear:

  • the decoded images may exhaust the available RAM;
  • the complete set of embeddings also consumes memory;
  • an interruption may force the entire process to start again.

To solve the first problem, we load only one batch of images at a time. It is important to understand that setting a batch_size in the model would not be enough if every photograph had already been opened and stored in a list before the method call.

for begin in range(start, len(paths), batch_size):
    end = min(begin + batch_size, len(paths))
    images = [
        load_rgb(path)
        for path in paths[begin:end]
    ]
    try:
            batch_embeddings = model.encode(
                images,
                batch_size=batch_size,
                normalize_embeddings=True,
                show_progress_bar=False,
            )
    finally:
        for image in images:
            image.close()

The finally block ensures that the files are closed even if a failure occurs during processing.

To address the second problem, we use numpy.memmap through the open_memmap method. Instead of keeping every embedding in RAM, we create a disk-backed array and write to it as each batch is completed.

embeddings = np.lib.format.open_memmap(
    embeddings_path,
    mode="w+",
    dtype=np.float32,
    shape=(len(paths), dimension),
)

embeddings[begin:end] = np.asarray(
    batch_embeddings,
    dtype=np.float32,
)
embeddings.flush()

As a result, memory usage is tied **primarily to the batch size rather than to the total number of images**.

Finally, we save a checkpoint at the end of each batch. It records the next position to be processed and allows the execution to resume after an interruption.

checkpoint_path.write_text(
    json.dumps(
        {**expected, "next_index": end},
        indent=2,
    ),
    encoding="utf-8",
)

However, saving only the position would not be safe. If an image were added, removed, or modified, the vectors could become associated with the wrong files. For this reason, **the checkpoint also contains a fingerprint calculated from the file paths, sizes, and modification dates, along with the model being used.**

def dataset_fingerprint(
    paths: list[Path],
    model_name: str,
) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(model_name.encode())

    for path in paths:
        stat = path.stat()
        digest.update(
            f"{path.resolve()}|{stat.st_size}|"
            f"{stat.st_mtime_ns}".encode()
        )

    return digest.hexdigest()

These three decisions (batch processing, disk-backed storage, and validated checkpoints) do not change the purpose of the project, but they allow it to become more than a demonstration that works only with a small number of photographs.

Cosine similarity

Once all the images have been transformed into vectors, we can compare them. The metric we will use is cosine similarity, which measures the angle between two vectors:

cosine_similarity(A, B) = (A · B) / (||A|| × ||B||)

The more closely aligned the vectors are, the greater their similarity. Because our embeddings have already been normalized, the denominator is equal to 1. Therefore, we can perform the calculation using a matrix product:

scores = left @ right.T

However, we once again face a scalability problem. A matrix containing every possible combination among N images has dimensions of N × N. For 100,000 images, this would represent 10 billion entries, even before considering any other processing structures.

For this reason, the implementation compares blocks of vectors and writes the resulting pairs directly to a CSV file:

for left_start in range(0, n, comparison_batch_size):
    left_end = min(
        left_start + comparison_batch_size,
        n,
    )
    left = np.asarray(
        embeddings[left_start:left_end]
    )

    for right_start in range(
        left_start,
        n,
        comparison_batch_size,
    ):
        right_end = min(
            right_start + comparison_batch_size,
            n,
        )
        right = np.asarray(
            embeddings[right_start:right_end]
        )
        scores = left @ right.T

This allows us to limit memory usage. It is important to note, however, that we are still performing all the comparisons. We have addressed the space problem, but the time complexity remains quadratic, or approximately O(N²).

For truly large collections, a natural evolution would be to use an approximate nearest neighbor index such as FAISS or HNSW and compare only the most likely neighbors of each image.

Similarity does not mean duplication

This brings us to an essential distinction: if two photographs have nearby embeddings, that does not necessarily mean they are identical.

Two different pictures of a beach may have high semantic similarity. Two consecutive photographs of the same person may also be very close, even though each one captures a unique moment.

Therefore, we also use pHash, or perceptual hashing. Unlike a cryptographic hash, it is designed to produce similar results for images that look alike.

hashes[begin:end] = [
    np.uint64(
        int(str(imagehash.phash(image)), 16)
    )
    for image in images
]

The distance between two hashes is calculated by counting the number of differing bits:

def phash_distance(
    a: np.uint64,
    b: np.uint64,
) -> int:
    return int(int(a ^ b).bit_count())

In the project, we classify a pair as probable_duplicate only when it meets two criteria simultaneously:

  • very high embedding similarity;
  • a small perceptual distance.

If only the first criterion is met, the pair is classified as semantically_similar.

probable_duplicate = (
    score >= duplicate_threshold
    and distance <= max_phash_distance
)

We use thresholds to make this classification, but they should only be treated as starting points. The best value depends on the model, the type of image, and the cost of each error. If a false positive could cause an important photograph to be lost, for example, the final decision must remain a human one.

A safer alternative would be to move candidate files to a quarantine folder, preserving a backup and allowing them to be reviewed before permanent deletion.

Visualizing the vector space

A CLIP embedding has far more than two dimensions. Because we cannot display that space directly in a chart, we need to reduce its dimensionality.

The project supports PCA and UMAP. PCA performs a linear projection that aims to preserve as much variance as possible. UMAP, on the other hand, is a nonlinear technique that tends to preserve certain local relationships between points more effectively.

However, we must be careful when interpreting the resulting figure. **The chart is not the original space: it is a projection, and some information is inevitably lost during the transformation.**

Projecting the entire collection may also consume a large amount of memory. For this reason, we select a reproducible sample:

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
indices = np.sort(
    rng.choice(
        len(paths),
        size=min(max_points, len(paths)),
        replace=False,
    )
)
sample = np.asarray(embeddings[indices])

We then apply the selected technique:

points = umap.UMAP(
    n_components=2,
    n_neighbors=max(
        2,
        min(15, len(sample) - 1),
    ),
    metric="cosine",
    random_state=7,
).fit_transform(sample)

Semantically related images are expected to appear in similar regions. However, the distance shown in the chart should not replace the metric calculated in the original vector space.

CLIP or SigLIP?

CLIP is a great choice for introducing multimodal embeddings, and it has broad support across libraries and examples. However, it is not the only option.

SigLIP also learns relationships between text and images, but it uses a sigmoid loss instead of the softmax-based contrastive formulation used by CLIP. In practice, different versions of these models may produce different results depending on the domain, language, resolution, and available infrastructure.

We should not choose a model simply because it leads a particular benchmark. For this problem, it would be useful to build a small evaluation dataset containing:

  • duplicate images with different compression levels and resolutions;
  • consecutive photographs of the same scene;
  • semantically similar images that should still be preserved;
  • visually similar but semantically different images;
  • real examples from the collection we want to organize.

We could then evaluate precision and recall at different thresholds, along with latency, throughput, memory usage, and embedding size.

Another important consideration is that vectors generated by different models do not necessarily belong to the same space. If the encoder changes, the collection must be processed again and its index rebuilt.

Conclusion

By transforming images into vectors, we can work with characteristics that go beyond their individual pixels. This allows us to visualize relationships between photographs and identify candidates that may be consuming unnecessary storage.

However, this experiment also reveals an important distinction: semantic similarity and duplication are not the same thing. Embeddings help us find related images, while pHash adds a signal of perceptual similarity. Even when both are used, automatic deletion still requires caution, calibration, and a recovery strategy.

We also saw that a seemingly simple solution quickly introduces engineering challenges. Loading every image, building a complete similarity matrix, and projecting every vector may work in a small demonstration, but they do not scale. Batch processing, disk-backed arrays, and checkpoints make the experiment more robust.

More than just a way to reduce the size of a photo folder, working with image embeddings is a practical way to understand how multimodal models organize information. Images stop being mere matrices of pixels and begin to occupy a mathematical space where we can compare meaning and uncover relationships that would be difficult to discover by comparing their pixels directly.

References

  • How to Measure Similarity Between SQL Queries Using Embeddings
  • Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
  • Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training
  • Image Search - Sentence Transformers documentation
  • UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction

title: Teaching AI Agents to Remember: ADRs, Specs, Engineering Decisions
partialText:
Teaching AI Agents to Remember: ADRs, Specs, Engineering Decisions — Part 2/5 of AI-Native Software Engineering Series

How to make architectural decisions part of your AI-assisted development workflow

In the previous article, I described a scenario where two AI-assisted pull requests were individually correct, yet together they overturned an intentional architectural decision.

AI Coding Assistant fixed the code but broke the architecture decision.

The first coding agent knew why the team had selected Option B.

The second agent didn’t.

The reviewing agent didn’t catch the reversal either.

This raises a practical question:

How do we make architectural decisions available to every developer and AI agent, without forcing people to repeatedly explain the same context?

My starting point would be Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), maintained directly in the GitHub repository.

This is not a new architecture practice. What’s changing is how valuable these records become when agents participate in planning, coding, and reviewing.

1. Start with lightweight ADRs

I wouldn’t document every coding decision.

Naming a variable, extracting a helper method, or fixing a straightforward bug generally doesn’t require an ADR.

But decisions that affect architecture, operating costs, data boundaries, security, integrations, or long-term maintainability are worth preserving.

A good test is:

Could a future developer reasonably undo this decision without understanding why it was made?

If yes, consider writing an ADR.

Michael Nygard’s widely used ADR approach includes four essential elements: status, context, decision, and consequences.

I would extend this slightly for AI-assisted engineering.

Example: Choosing CPU processing over GPU processing

# ADR-001: Use CPU-Based Processing
Status: Accepted
Date: 2026-10-18
Owner: <dev name>
Related work: ARCH-142

## Context
We evaluated two approaches for processing documents in 10th Oct 2026's team's standup.
Option A: GPU-based processing
- Lower processing latency
- Requires dedicated GPU infrastructure
- Higher fixed operating cost
Option B: CPU-based processing
- Higher processing latency
- Uses existing infrastructure
- Lower and more predictable cost
Our current infrastructure budget does not
support dedicated GPU capacity.

## Decision
Use Option B for document processing.

## Consequences
- Accept higher processing latency.
- Avoid dedicated GPU infrastructure costs.
- Monitor latency and processing costs.

## Reconsider When
- GPU infrastructure becomes affordable.
- Processing latency violates the approved SLA.
- Workload volume materially changes.

## Applies To
- services/document-processing/**
- infrastructure/document-processing/**

## Supersedes
None

The important part isn’t the Markdown format.

It’s that a future developer, coding agent, or reviewer can understand the reasoning without reconstructing an old meeting.

An ADR should be concise enough to read and specific enough to prevent an expensive misunderstanding.

2. Keep decisions discoverable in GitHub

A simple starting structure could look like this:

repository/
│
├── AGENTS.md
│
├── docs/
│   └── decisions/
│       ├── INDEX.md
│       ├── ADR-001-cpu-processing.md
│       ├── ADR-002-storage-strategy.md
│       └── ADR-003-event-driven-processing.md
│
└── .github/
    ├── copilot-instructions.md
    └── instructions/
        └── architecture.instructions.md

Each file has a different responsibility.

  • ADRs preserve the actual decisions and their rationale.
  • INDEX.md is a lightweight catalog that helps developers and agents discover relevant decisions.
  • AGENTS.md communicates standing guidance to coding agents.
  • Copilot instructions provide repository-wide or path-specific context to GitHub Copilot, including review expectations.

I would avoid duplicating full decisions across these files. Multiple conflicting copies of the same rule create another maintenance problem.

An example INDEX.md

In the actual Markdown file, each ADR ID would link to its corresponding document.

I prefer stable ADR IDs rather than making a story or bug ID the primary identifier.

A user story may be completed in one sprint.

An architectural decision may influence dozens of features over several years.

Keep the story ID as a reference, but let the decision have its own identity.

3. Make agents consult decisions before making changes

The next step is connecting these records to the agent workflow.

For example, an AGENTS.md file might include:

# Engineering Decision Guidance
Before planning or modifying code:
1. Identify the components and files affected.
2. Read docs/decisions/INDEX.md.
3. Open applicable accepted ADRs.
4. Identify architectural constraints and trade-offs.
5. Include relevant ADR IDs in the implementation plan.
6. Do not silently overturn an accepted decision.
7. If a decision appears outdated or conflicts with
   the task, flag it and propose reconsideration.
8. In the final summary, report ADRs consulted
   and any potential conflicts.
Treat ADRs as decision context, not as permanently
unchangeable rules.

The exact instruction mechanism depends on the AI tool.

GitHub Copilot supports repository-wide instructions in .github/copilot-instructions.md, path-specific instructions in .github/instructions/, and agent instructions through AGENTS.md.

However, support and instruction precedence vary by feature and environment. Teams should verify which instructions their coding and reviewing agents actually consume.

That last detail matters.

Adding a file doesn’t prove an agent read or followed it.

A responsible workflow should require visible evidence of which decisions were consulted.

4. Make decision awareness part of pull requests

I would add three fields to the pull request template:

## Architectural Decision Impact

Relevant ADRs:
- ADR-001
Does this PR change an accepted decision?
- [ ] No
- [ ] Yes
- [ ] Uncertain
If yes or uncertain, explain:
...
Verification evidence:
...

This does two things.

First, it encourages developers and agents to actively consider existing decisions.

Second, it makes potential conflicts visible to reviewers without requiring them to reconstruct the entire architectural history.

For example, imagine Copilot recommends switching CPU processing to GPU processing.

The PR should not simply say:

“Improved throughput by replacing CPU processing.”

It should identify the architectural conflict:

“ADR-001 selected CPU processing due to infrastructure budget constraints. This PR proposes GPU processing and therefore requires reconsideration of that decision.”

Now the reviewer knows what question to ask.

Not just “Does this code work?”

But “Has the reason for the original decision changed?”

5. Avoid turning every implementation into an approval bottleneck

One obvious objection is that this creates more process.

If every developer must write a plan, find an architect, schedule a review, and wait for approval, we may lose much of the productivity AI provides.

I wouldn’t require that.

Instead, I’d use risk-based review.

  • Routine implementation: The agent identifies relevant decisions and proceeds when the change stays within approved constraints.
  • Material architectural change: The agent creates a short plan, explains the trade-off, and requests review from developer. If the change is significant, it should be reviewed with team.
  • Conflict with an accepted decision: The agent proposes an ADR amendment or a new superseding ADR before changing the architecture.

The objective is not to add human approval everywhere.

It is to reserve human attention for decisions that genuinely change the system’s intended behavior, cost, or risk.

6. What if an ADR becomes outdated?

This is where many ADR practices fail.

A team documents a decision once, treats it as permanent, and eventually builds a repository full of stale instructions.

Let’s return to ADR-001.

Suppose GPU costs fall substantially six months later.

Option A may now be both faster and economically viable.

Should the agent ignore this opportunity because the ADR says to use Option B?

No.

It should challenge the assumptions behind the decision.

A useful proposal might say:

ADR-001 selected CPU processing because GPU infrastructure exceeded the approved budget. Updated cost estimates suggest the original constraint may no longer apply. Recommend reconsidering the decision before migration.

The team can then evaluate the evidence and, if appropriate, create a new ADR.

# ADR-008: Adopt GPU-Based Processing
Status: Accepted
Supersedes: ADR-001

## Context
GPU infrastructure costs have decreased.
Updated benchmarks indicate that GPU processing
now meets our operating budget.

## Decision
Move document processing to GPU infrastructure.

## Consequences
- Reduced processing latency.
- New infrastructure and monitoring requirements.
- Migration and rollback plan required.

ADR-001 stays in the repository, marked Superseded.

We don’t delete history.

We preserve the reasoning behind both decisions.

7. How it is different than spec-driven development?

If you’ve used spec-driven development (SDD), this might sound familiar. Tools like GitHub’s Spec Kit have you write a spec, generate a plan, break it into tasks, then implement. Isn’t that the same thing?

No, They answer different questions.

  • A spec answers: what are we building, and how, for this feature? It looks forward and is scoped to one piece of work.
  • An ADR answers: what did we already decide, and why? It looks backward, and it outlives any single feature.

Here is how I think about it: the constitution is the bylaws, specs are the work orders, and ADRs are the case law.

They connect in two places. Specs read ADRs as constraints before planning. And when a plan makes a decision that passes the “could someone undo this without knowing why” test, it gets promoted to an ADR.

SDD gives agents direction. ADRs give them memory. Specs without decision memory just produce well-formatted reversals.

8. Capture decisions throughout the engineering lifecycle

Architectural decisions don’t happen only while coding.

They happen in planning meetings, incident reviews, design discussions, pull requests, and production investigations.

I’d establish a simple habit:

Whenever the team makes a significant decision, someone proposes an ADR or updates an existing one.

AI can help draft the record from approved meeting notes or technical discussions, but a proposed summary should not become an accepted decision without the appropriate confirmation.

Over time, the repository starts retaining something more valuable than implementation history.

It retains engineering reasoning.

My takeaway

We don’t need every AI agent to remember every conversation.

We need every agent to reliably discover the decisions relevant to the work it is performing.

ADRs are a practical starting point.

But the long-term direction is broader: persistent engineering context, explicit decision authority, and independently verifiable constraints.

That’s the foundation of an engineering system where agents can do more than generate code.

They can make changes while respecting the organization’s accumulated judgment.

And that leads to the next question:

What happens when we connect planning, coding, reviewing, testing, and deployment into one coordinated autonomous system?

That’s where software factories enter the picture, see you in part 3!
